lines.note: Jooroo denotes a noble person; the paired jooroo and geroo contrast high and low rank. The worn initial is I. Enlarged inspection shows Paßoa, with a printed a and the double-s ligature, rather than silently regularizing the word to peſſoa.
The divided Gẽ-te completes the description of people of high and low standing. Item introduces a second sense of jooroo, specifically a woman of rank.
Honrada completes molher honrada, a woman of respectable or noble standing. This short continuation is a separate physical row.
Jooron is explained through arasoi ronzuru, disputing or arguing; the Portuguese gives disputa and porfia. The scan supports initial I rather than a long s.
Jooruri is glossed as a pure jewel and a precious blue stone. The entry concerns the stone, not the later theatrical genre; precio- continues below.
The continuation completes preciosa azul: a precious blue stone. It belongs to the jewel entry and is not an independent fragment.
Joosaku denotes outstanding workmanship, glossed as obra prima. The divided cata- begins the sword example on the next row.

runs.text: He Catana que fez algum inſigne

lines.note: Cata-na nari completes the Japanese example; the Portuguese describes a sword made by a distinguished craftsman. Catana occurs within the Portuguese explanation and is eligible for whole-word typeface review.
Official completes the previous description of a distinguished craftsman. Here the word denotes a skilled practitioner, not a government official.

runs.text: O eſtimar, ou fazer caſo das peſſoas ſe-

lines.note: Ioſai concerns valuing or showing regard to persons according to rank, before the explanation of contrary usage below. The initial I is restored; enlargement resolves the long-ſ/t ligature in eſtimar.

runs.text: gundo o grao, & calidade de cada hũa. S.

lines.note: Completes segundo: people are valued according to each person’s rank and quality. The final S. marks written usage, before the contrast with everyday speech.

runs.text: mas na pratica ſe toma em ſentido contrario.

lines.note: The compiler explicitly says that practical usage takes the expression in the opposite sense. This qualification is essential to interpreting the following negative examples.
Josaini senu and vomowanu are alternative negative expressions: not treating someone carelessly or thinking little of them. The printed l introduces the alternative.

runs.text: ter em pouco, ou não deixar de eſtimar, como

lines.note: The Portuguese expands the negatives as not despising someone and not failing to show due regard. This continues the example, not the initial positive definition alone.
Conuem closes the previous translation. Josaimo gozaranu begins another example denying any deficiency or neglect in proper courtesy.

runs.text: auer falta, nem deſcuido nas corteſias deui-

lines.note: The translation specifies absence of failure or negligence in the courtesies owed. Deui- is a physical word division, completed by das below.
Das completes deuidas, followed by &c. The short row closes the courtesy example before the next headword.
Joosoo is paraphrased as speaking upward to a superior, camiye mooxi aguru. The Portuguese likewise describes addressing a noble person; the caron and circumflex are distinct printed marks.
Completes the divided peſ-ſoa nobre, the noble person addressed. The attached a in the preceding apeſ- is retained as printed spacing.

runs.text: Iǒte, l, jǒteno mono. i, Iǒzu.

lines.note: Joote and jooteno mono are equated with joozu, a person skilled at something. Deſtro corrects OCR Detro; the opening separator is visibly a comma.
Algũa couſa completes the description of competence in some activity. The tilde is over u, not the final a.

runs.text: Iǒten. Tenno vye, l, tenni noboru.

lines.note: Jooten is explained both as being above the heavens and as ascending to heaven. The alternative marker separates tenno vye from tenni noboru.

runs.text: cima dos ceos, ou ſubir ao ceo. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the two Portuguese senses and introduces jooten suru. The example prints a tilde over e, Iǒtẽ, abbreviating the nasal rather than omitting it without a mark.
The first translation means ascending to heaven. The next Japanese example begins with Jesus Christ and an honorific expression for the Ascension.

runs.text: Ieſu Chriſto ſubio a os ceos.

lines.note: Naſareta completes the honorific Japanese example; the Portuguese says that Jesus Christ ascended to heaven. Its spaced a os is preserved rather than contracted.

runs.text: Cidade metropole, ou principal do reino.

lines.note: Jooto denotes a metropolis or chief city of a kingdom. The initial I is visible beside the rule and must not be dropped.
Jootoo is paraphrased by masani vqetamawaru, hearing or receiving what is said. The first o has a circumflex and the second a caron; they are not regularized.

runs.text: ceber o que ſe diz. S.

lines.note: Completes perceber o que ſe diz, understanding what is said. The final S. identifies written usage.
Jootoo shoogaku is glossed as becoming a Buddha. Fotoque is Japanese embedded in a Portuguese sentence; Bup. labels Buddhist usage, not part of the Japanese phrase.
Joosen means boarding a boat, funeni noru. The crop clearly supports noru rather than OCR notu; the illustrative suru construction continues below.
Joosen suru supplies the verbal construction for embarking. The damaged vowel after ſ is read as u in agreement with the visible form and the preceding boarding gloss, not OCR ſeru.

runs.text: Paraiſo que os gentios cuidão q̃ ha.

lines.note: Jooset is a paradise said by the compiler to be believed in by non-Christians. The religious characterization belongs to the historical gloss, not an independent assertion by this review.
Jooshi is explained as a message or commission from a person of high standing. Vyeno tçucai gives the Japanese paraphrase.
Jooshin is equated with xinzuru, offering or sending something to a person of rank. Oferecer is visibly one word; the OCR’s internal space is removed.

runs.text: gũa couſa a peſſoa honrada. S.

lines.note: Completes algũa couſa a peſſoa honrada, something offered to an honoured person. The S. is a written-register label.
A separate jooshin entry denotes a constant heart or disposition, tçuneno cocoro. The headword’s abraded initial I remains visible beside the rule.
Completes immudauel and adds equal or steady. Jooshinna fito begins the example of a person possessing that constancy.
Conſtante and inuariauel complete the description of the steadfast person. This is the second jooshin entry, not the offering verb above.
Jooshiki is given the terse gloss pertinacia, obstinacy or stubborn persistence. The initial is a worn capital I, not OCR long ſ.
Jooshikina describes a stubborn, obstinate person. The initial I is restored from visible traces, while the printed adjectival form remains unchanged.
Jooshikini is identified as the adverb corresponding to the two preceding forms. Adu. is a grammatical label, not a separate Portuguese definition.
Jooshit denotes loss through burning, explained by yaqi vxinǒ. The Portuguese word quei-ma is physically divided; the Japanese final t is not expanded.
Iyeuo jooshit itaita illustrates losing a house or houses in a fire. The Portuguese begins “I lost some houses”; the printed historical inflection itaita is retained.
Completes the example with houses that burned down. The historical ending queimarão is preserved rather than modernized.
Jooshoku denotes a high office or position. The example begins with the divided headword Iǒxo-cu and contrasts it with low office.
Jooshoku and geshoku are both accepted without aversion in the example. Qirauazu is the negative form of disliking or rejecting.

runs.text: repugnancia a officios altos nem baixos.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the example as having no reluctance toward either high or low offices. The column ends after a complete sentence.
Jooshu is the lord of a castle, xirono nuxi. The initial and complete right-hand gloss are present in the crop; the headword is not a continuation.

runs.text: Peßoa principal, ou como cabeça dos

lines.note: A separate jooshu denotes a principal person or head of others. This independent entry begins at the column margin.
Outros completes “head of the others.” The damaged central letters are recoverable, and the row is distinct from the next three-part classification.
Jooshu, booshu and kashu introduce a classification by the direction of the head. The repeated jooshu starts the first definition, not a duplicate caused by OCR.

runs.text: tem a cabeça pera cima como os homens;

lines.note: The first class has its head directed upward, as humans do. Bǒ- begins the second class; the separator before it is a semicolon.

runs.text: Os de mais animaes que tem a cabeça pe-

lines.note: Bǒ-xu is completed and defined as the other animals whose heads face sideways. The Portuguese pe- continues as pera below.
Completes the sideways orientation, then defines kashu as plants. The Japanese class-name is a standalone label rather than a word embedded syntactically in the Portuguese sentence.
Plants are described as having their head, or root, in the earth. This finishes the three-way classification without imposing a modern biological taxonomy.
Jooye is clean clothing, isaguiyoi coromo. The damaged m in coromo has a detached right stem; the clear coromo in the next entry supplies a local comparator, supporting coromo over OCR corono.
A separate jooye is an outer or upper garment, vyeno coromo. Its intact coromo helps interpret the damaged occurrence immediately above.
Jooyo is transferring an inheritance, paraphrased as yuzzuri atayuru. The doubled z is preserved rather than converted to modern romanization.
Joyo is glossed as wild yams, yamano imo. Unlike the adjacent entries, the headword’s first o is unaccented in the print.

runs.text: Dilatar, ou encarecer com palauras. S.

lines.note: Joyoo denotes enlarging on something in words or speaking of it with emphasis. The final circumflex and written-register S. are retained.
Joyomen names a particular prepared dish, but the Portuguese supplies no ingredients. The transcription therefore does not impose a more precise culinary identification.
Jooyuu is a castle and settlement, xiro and ſato, with a written-register label. The final u bears its own length mark.

runs.text: Laya de religioſos baixos ẽtre os Xǒdǒxùs.

lines.note: Jooza denotes a lower grade of religious among the Xǒdǒxùs. The sect-name is embedded in Portuguese; enlarged reading supports two caroned o vowels and d rather than OCR õdb.
Joozu is skillfulness, explained by vuate and jooteno mono. This repeats the equivalent used earlier in column 1, confirming the entry’s practical sense.
Algũa couſa completes the statement that someone is skilled in an activity. The next material is a new consonantal-I section, not part of this entry.
Ju is glossed through yomi,u, reading, followed by jusuru as an example. The large I and adjacent V together form IV; the enlarged I spans this row and the next, so its owning crop is taller.
Juuaku means the ten evils, touono acu. The small I begins a separate headword below IV; neither the enlarged I beside it nor the damaged u should become the OCR string lIbacu.

runs.text: Mǒgo, qigo, accô, riǒjet, xexxǒ, chǔ-

lines.note: Begins the ten-evils list with false speech, frivolous speech, abusive speech, double-tongued speech, killing and the first part of theft. The Japanese list is kept in its printed order, not rearranged to a familiar modern enumeration.
Completes chǔ-tǒ and adds sexual misconduct, greed, anger and ignorance. Mẽ- begins the Portuguese translation mentira across the physical line break.

runs.text: tira, palauras de zombaria, ou liſonjas, pala-

lines.note: The Portuguese begins with lying, mocking or flattering words, and the start of injurious words. It translates the preceding list rather than introducing new headwords.

runs.text: uras injurioſas, o falar perduas bocas, matar

lines.note: Completes injurious words, adds speaking with two mouths, and begins the prohibition on killing a living thing. The historical joined perduas is retained.

runs.text: couſa viua, furtar, luxuria, cobiça, ira, ig-

lines.note: Continues with killing, theft, lust, greed and anger, followed by divided ig-norancia. The scan supports luxuria with x, correcting OCR lucuria.
Norancia completes ignorancia, the final item in the ten-evils gloss. The short continuation closes the list before juubun.

runs.text: Perfeição de couſa que lhe não falta

lines.note: Juubun is completeness, specifically a thing lacking nothing. The Portuguese definition continues on the next row.
Nada completes the absence of any deficiency. Juubunno doorigia is translated as an adequate or fully sufficient reason.
Adequada closes that example. Juubun nareba vchi coboſu begins a proverb about a full vessel spilling; the final verb is physically divided.

runs.text: Estãdo algũa couſa chea logo ſe entorna.

lines.note: Completes coboſu and states that a full thing promptly spills. The crop supports entorna, with r+n, rather than OCR entoma.

runs.text: Prou. Aplicaſe a gente, cidade, &c. que eſ-

lines.note: Prou. explicitly labels the saying a proverb and begins its application to people, cities and similar entities. The final eſ- continues below.

runs.text: tando muito farta, & proſpera lhe ſobreuem

lines.note: Explains the state of abundance and prosperity before misfortune arrives. No sentence-ending point is visible after ſobreuem; the syntax continues directly into the next row.
Completes the proverb’s explanation: hardship or scarcity commonly follows excessive prosperity. This is the compiler’s explanation of the saying.

runs.text: Copo, ou pucaro que depois de eſtar

lines.note: Juubunpai is a cup or drinking vessel that behaves unusually when completely filled. The definition continues rather than ending after eſtar.

runs.text: cheo totalmente ſe lhe vai o vinho, ou agoa

lines.note: Once the vessel is full, its wine or water drains away. The conjunction ou distinguishes alternative contents, not two different vessels.
The liquid goes downward and disappears, completing the cup’s description. The gloss alone does not require adding a particular mechanical design.
Jukai is receiving precepts, imaximeuo vquru. The Portuguese begins the explanation of religious admission or ordination.

runs.text: & leis quãdo ſe hũ rapa, ou ſe faz religioſo.

lines.note: The precepts and rules are received when someone shaves the head or becomes religious. Hũ is the abbreviated indefinite pronoun, not a Japanese word.

runs.text: Estar viuo, ou com vida. S.

lines.note: Jukoo is being alive, stated twice in Portuguese as living or having life. The final S. marks written usage.
Jukon and jukkon denote close friendship and association. The alternative preserves the doubled c rather than selecting a single normalized form.
Completes intimate communication with someone, then begins the example with Pedroto, “with Pedro.” The name and attached Japanese particle are roman, including the initial P.
Pedroni juccõ xita is the alternative construction for becoming close friends with Pedro. The tilde abbreviates the final nasal of jukkon; the printed initial P is roman.

runs.text: ou trauei grande amizade com Pedro.

lines.note: The Portuguese finishes with forming a great friendship with Pedro. Both clauses translate the same Japanese example.
Jukkei is glossed through qidocunaru facaricoto, a notably ingenious plan. Induſ- begins the Portuguese definition, whose continuation is anticipated by the bottom catchword and resumes on f295.
